questions.question_text: Who bears ultimate responsibility for proper handling of escrow deposits in Virginia?
questions.correct_answer: The principal broker of the firm
distractors: The salesperson who drafted the contract
The office manager at the branch location
The settlement attorney handling the closing
questions.explanation: Under 18VAC135-20-181 the principal broker is held responsible for the firm's escrow accounts and must have signatory authority on them. A supervising broker or any other licensee with signatory authority may also be held responsible.

questions.question_text: A buyer submits an earnest money deposit on Tuesday. The contract is ratified Thursday. By when must the broker deposit the funds?
questions.correct_answer: By end of the following Thursday
distractors: By end of the following Tuesday
Within 24 hours of receiving the check
By end of the next calendar day
questions.explanation: Earnest money must be placed in escrow by the end of the fifth business banking day following ratification, unless the principals to the transaction agree otherwise in writing (18VAC135-20-181). Ratification on Thursday puts the fifth business banking day on the following Thursday.

questions.question_text: A broker receives a $10,000 earnest money check. Where must the funds be deposited?
questions.correct_answer: A federally insured escrow account in the firm's licensed name
distractors: Any account the broker chooses if records are kept
The broker's personal savings account
The listing agent's individual client account
questions.explanation: Each firm must maintain one or more federally insured escrow accounts in the name by which the firm is licensed, with the accounts, checks, and bank statements labeled 'escrow' and designated as escrow accounts with the financial institution (18VAC135-20-181). The regulation does not require the depository to be located in Virginia.

questions.question_text: An agent receives earnest money but the contract has not yet been ratified. When does the deposit deadline begin?
questions.correct_answer: The five-day clock starts at ratification
distractors: The clock starts when the agent receives the check
The clock starts when the offer is first submitted
The clock starts at the listing agreement date
questions.explanation: The five-business-banking-day clock in 18VAC135-20-181 runs from contract ratification, not from the date the licensee physically receives the check. The principals may agree to a different timeline in writing.

questions.question_text: Which designation must appear on a Virginia brokerage escrow bank account?
questions.correct_answer: It must be labeled as escrow or trust
distractors: It must include the broker's personal name
It must reference the specific property address
It must show the client's Social Security number
questions.explanation: The account, its checks, and its bank statements must be labeled 'escrow' and the account designated as an escrow account with the financial institution, so client funds are clearly distinguished from the firm's operating funds (18VAC135-20-181).

questions.question_text: A Virginia broker leaves earned commission funds in the firm's escrow account for eight months after closing. Is this permitted?
questions.correct_answer: No, licensee funds must be withdrawn at least every six months
distractors: Yes, earned funds may remain indefinitely
Yes, if the amount stays under $500
No, licensee funds may never be in the account at all
questions.explanation: Commingling is prohibited, but funds that will ultimately belong to the licensee may stay in the escrow account if they are separately identified and withdrawn at intervals of not more than six months (18VAC135-20-181). Virginia's regulation sets no flat dollar allowance for the broker's own funds.

questions.question_text: What is commingling in the context of Virginia escrow accounts?
questions.correct_answer: Mixing broker personal funds with client funds
distractors: Depositing earnest money in a federally insured bank
Holding deposits from multiple transactions together
Transferring funds between two escrow accounts
questions.explanation: Commingling is mixing a broker's personal or business operating funds with client escrow funds, which 18VAC135-20-181 prohibits. The only funds of the licensee that may sit in the account are amounts that will ultimately belong to the licensee, and only if separately identified and withdrawn at least every six months.

questions.question_text: A buyer and seller both want the escrow deposit placed in an interest-bearing account. What must the broker obtain?
questions.correct_answer: Written agreement from all parties stating who gets interest
distractors: Verbal consent from the buyer only
Approval from the Virginia Real Estate Board
A court order authorizing the interest arrangement
questions.explanation: An interest-bearing escrow account is permitted only when written disclosure is made in the contract of purchase or lease to all principals regarding the disbursement of interest, so the parties must agree in writing on who receives it (18VAC135-20-181).

questions.question_text: A brokerage firm is dissolving. What must the principal broker do with escrow funds?
questions.correct_answer: Properly dispose of all escrow funds before dissolving
distractors: Transfer all escrow funds to the Virginia Board
Distribute funds equally among remaining agents
Convert the escrow account to a personal account
questions.explanation: On dissolution the principal broker must ensure proper disposition of all escrow funds — returning deposits to the rightful parties or transferring them to a successor under Va. Code § 54.1-2108.2 — before the escrow account is closed.

questions.question_text: A seller asks the broker to place escrow funds into a non-interest-bearing account. The buyer wants interest. What should the broker do?
questions.correct_answer: Use a non-interest-bearing account since all parties must agree
distractors: Follow the buyer's preference as depositor of funds
Follow the seller's preference as property owner
Split the deposit between two separate accounts
questions.explanation: An interest-bearing escrow account requires written disclosure and agreement of all principals under 18VAC135-20-181. Because the seller does not agree, the broker must use a standard non-interest-bearing escrow account.

questions.question_text: How long must a Virginia broker retain escrow account records?
distractors: Five years
Seven years
Ten years
questions.explanation: A complete and accurate record of money received on behalf of others and its disbursement must be kept for three years from the date of closing, or from termination of the transaction or lease (18VAC135-20-185). Brokerage agreements and dual/designated agency disclosures are likewise kept three years from execution.

questions.question_text: Under Virginia's Real Estate Board regulations, when must a firm's principal or supervising broker conduct an audit of the firm's practices?
questions.correct_answer: Within 90 days prior to expiration of the firm license
distractors: Only when the Board opens an investigation
Every six months regardless of renewal date
Only if the firm holds escrow funds over $50,000
questions.explanation: The principal or supervising broker must conduct, or have a third party conduct, an audit within 90 days prior to expiration of the firm license, covering escrow handling, fair housing, advertising, agency, disclosures, and use of unlicensed personnel (18VAC135-20-225). Va. Code § 54.1-2106.2 requires certification of that audit on renewal, and self-reported findings can qualify for immunity under the voluntary compliance program.

questions.question_text: A buyer and seller dispute who is entitled to a $15,000 earnest money deposit. What legal action can the broker take?
questions.correct_answer: File an interpleader action with the court
distractors: Return the full amount to the buyer immediately
Split the deposit equally between both parties
Hold the funds indefinitely until they agree
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2108.2 lets a broker holding a disputed deposit file an interpleader action under § 16.1-77 so the court takes custody and determines the rightful recipient. The other options are release on the parties' written agreement, release under a court order, or release under the contract's clear and explicit terms — and a broker who complies with the section is immune from liability to the parties.

questions.question_text: During a review, the Board finds that a broker's escrow records from a closing two years ago are incomplete. What is the likely consequence?
questions.correct_answer: Disciplinary action for inadequate record keeping
distractors: No violation since records are under five years old
A warning letter with no further consequences
Automatic license revocation by the Board
questions.explanation: Complete and accurate escrow records must be kept for three years from closing (18VAC135-20-185). Records that are incomplete anywhere inside that retention window are a violation subject to Board disciplinary action.

questions.question_text: A broker filed an interpleader for disputed escrow funds. Who decides how the funds are distributed?
questions.correct_answer: The court determines the rightful recipient
distractors: The principal broker makes the final decision
The Virginia Real Estate Board holds a hearing
The listing agent decides based on contract terms
questions.explanation: In an interpleader action under Va. Code § 54.1-2108.2 the broker deposits the disputed funds with the court, which determines the rightful recipient. A broker who complies with the statute is immune from liability to the parties to the contract.
